Empirical Research Plan  
“Mortality and Health Effects of Early-2000s Adult Medicaid Expansions”

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Strategy: Difference-in-Differences (DID) with an event-study extension in a two-way-fixed-effects (TWFE) framework.

Why appropriate  
• Treatment varies across states (AZ, ME, NY) and over time (2001–2002).  
• Outcomes are available annually (mortality) or in repeated cross-sections (CPS, BRFSS).  
• No obvious running variable suitable for RDD; expansions are statewide policy shocks not driven by an instrument.  
• DID exploits within-state changes net of common shocks captured by year FEs and time-invariant differences captured by county (or individual-residence) FEs.  
• Event study lets us (i) test the parallel-trends assumption and (ii) trace dynamic effects.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment definition  
• ​Treated unit: A person (or county-year-demographic cell) located in Arizona, Maine, or New York.  
• ​Treatment variable: Treat_s = 1 if state ∈ {AZ, ME, NY}, else 0.  
• ​Post_st = 1 for years ≥ the first month of coverage for childless adults (state-specific: NY 2001, AZ 2001, ME 2002).  
• Main DID variable = Treat_s × Post_st.

Control group  
• Neighboring comparison states with no contemporaneous eligibility change: Nevada, New Mexico, New Hampshire, Pennsylvania.  
• In robustness checks, (i) drop each control state one-at-a-time, (ii) include the rest of the US except the three treated states, and (iii) restrict to bordering counties only.

Timing  
NY: September 2001 → treat_post=1 for 2002 onward (drop 2001 as mixed).  
AZ: November 2001 → treat_post=1 for 2002 onward.  
ME: October 2002 → treat_post=1 for 2003 onward.  
Event-study relative year k = Year – First-full-year-of-expansion_s (k = …–5, –4, …, +5).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Parallel trends: In the absence of expansion, outcomes in treated and control states would have evolved similarly.  
Plausibility: Neighboring states are similar economically and demographically; five-year pre-period allows visual and statistical pre-trend tests.

A2. No concurrent, treated-state-specific shocks that directly affect outcomes.  
Plausibility: We know of no other large, adult-health insurance reforms in AZ/ME/NY during 2000-2005; we will control for county-year economic covariates and check policy databases for other changes.

A3. Stable Unit Treatment Value (no cross-state spillovers).  
Plausibility: Low-income adults are unlikely to migrate across states for Medicaid within the five-year window; cross-border care spillovers minimal because Medicaid is state-specific.

A4. Composition stability: Expansion does not induce selective in- or out-migration that would mechanically drive mortality.  
Plausibility: Short horizon and administratively complex relocation for Medicaid make large migration unlikely; we will test this with CPS interstate mobility data.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Main Threats & Mitigation
--------------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Differential pre-trends (violation of A1).  
• Mitigation: Event-study estimates, formal F-tests on leads; add state-specific linear trends; synthetic control robustness.

T2. September 11, 2001 mortality shock uniquely affecting New York.  
• Mitigation: (i) Drop New York City counties in robustness check; (ii) drop 2001 altogether; (iii) include county-specific time trends; (iv) compare results with and without NY.

T3. Economic recession 2001–2002 hitting treated states differently.  
• Mitigation: Control for county-year unemployment, poverty and income; interact those covariates with Treat_s to allow differential impacts; weight by county population to reduce influence of small counties.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline  (executable after data are saved as CSVs)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 0. Packages
# ------------------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)    # fast data wrangling
library(fixest)        # TWFE regressions
library(ggplot2)       # event-study plot
# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Load data
# ------------------------------------------------------------
mort <- fread("mortality.csv")      # county-year demographic cells
cps  <- fread("cps_individual.csv") # individual-level
brf  <- fread("brfss_individual.csv")

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Construct treatment variables (mortality example)
# ------------------------------------------------------------
treat_states <- c("AZ","ME","NY")
control_states <- c("NV","NM","NH","PA")

# First full year of expansion per state
exp_year <- data.table(state=c("AZ","ME","NY"),
                       expyr=c(2002,2003,2002))

mort <- merge(mort, exp_year, by="state", all.x=TRUE)

mort[, treat := fifelse(state %in% treat_states,1,0)]
mort[, post  := fifelse(year >= expyr & !is.na(expyr),1,0)]
mort[, did   := treat*post]

# Event-study relative year
mort[, rel_year := ifelse(treat==1, year - expyr, NA)]
mort <- mort[rel_year >= -5 & rel_year <= 5] # keep symmetric window

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Control covariates
# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Assuming mort already has pov_rate, unemp_rate, med_income
# optional: scale covariates

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Main DID regression
# ------------------------------------------------------------
did_mod <- feols(death_rate ~ did + pov_rate + unemp_rate + med_income |
                   county + year,
                 data = mort,
                 weights = ~population,
                 cluster = ~state)

summary(did_mod)

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 5. Event-study
# ------------------------------------------------------------
es_mod <- feols(death_rate ~ i(rel_year, treat, ref=-1) + pov_rate + unemp_rate + med_income |
                  county + year,
                data = mort, weights = ~population,
                cluster = ~state)

iplot(es_mod, main = "Event-study: Adult Mortality", xlab="Years relative to expansion")

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 6. Robustness: add county-specific linear trends
# ------------------------------------------------------------
mort[, ctrend := year*1.0]    # numeric
did_trend <- feols(death_rate ~ did + pov_rate + unemp_rate + med_income |
                     county + year + county:ctrend,
                   data = mort, weights = ~population,
                   cluster = ~state)

summary(did_trend)
```

(Analogous code for CPS and BRFSS outcomes, with individual-level weights and clustering at state.)

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Insurance coverage: +10 to +15 percentage-point increase in Medicaid coverage, –8 to –12 pp drop in uninsurance for low-income adults.  
Mortality: 4–6 percent reduction in all-cause mortality among 20-64 year-olds (≈ –2 deaths per 100,000).  
Cost-related delays: decline of ~5 pp.  
Self-rated “fair/poor” health: fall of 3 pp.  
Theory: Insurance improves access, earlier detection, and financial protection, translating into modest yet measurable short-run mortality declines and better self-reported health.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DID)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
C1. Pre-treatment trends parallel? …… 1  
C2. No confounding policy shocks? …… 0.5 (9/11 in NY)  
C3. No spillovers / SUTVA? ……………… 1  
C4. Stable composition of units? ……… 0.5 (possible migration)  
C5. Treatment timing exogenous? …… 1  

Overall score: 4/5 (reasonable but not perfect)
